messages.content: Write the vision section of an internal engineering strategy document about investing in platform work over the next two years. Around 250 words.

output:
Passes both gates (slopwatch, codewatch), 260 words.

## Vision

By September 2028, a team here can take a new backend service from an empty repository to production traffic in a week, and spend none of that week on logging, deploys, secret rotation, or a Postgres schema. Today the same path takes five to six weeks. Four of them go to rebuilding what three other teams have already built, slightly differently each time.

Closing that gap is the whole case for platform investment. We are not proposing a platform team as an end in itself. We are proposing to pay down a tax that every product team currently pays in full, in private, with no shared benefit when they finish.

Concretely, two years out we want three things to be true. First, one paved road exists for service scaffolding, CI, and observability, and at least 80% of production services ride it. Second, an on-call engineer debugging an incident reads one set of dashboards, not seven per-team variants. Third, the platform team's own backlog is driven by measured friction — deploy lead time, failed first deploys, time-to-first-log — rather than by whoever asks loudest.

We should be honest about the trade. For roughly the first nine months, platform work will slow feature delivery, because the people who know the existing systems best are the people who have to build the replacement. We think that cost is worth paying, and we would rather state it here than discover it in a quarterly review.

The test of this strategy is boring: in 2028, does anyone still write their own deploy pipeline?

---

The numbers (five to six weeks, 80%, nine months) are placeholders — swap in your real baseline before this circulates, since the argument leans on them.
